text: A firewall rule or IDS signature almost always has to make a judgment call, because the traffic it evaluates could legitimately be either benign or malicious. A spike in outbound connections might be a backup job or data exfiltration. A login from an unusual location might be a traveling employee or a stolen credential.

That judgment work is exactly why SOCs drown in alert volume — most of what fires just looks ambiguous enough to need a second look. A honeypot or deception alert skips that ambiguity entirely, because nothing legitimate should ever touch it. A firewall alert might be legitimate traffic that looks suspicious; a honeypot alert, by definition, has no legitimate explanation at all.

No real user or process was ever configured to generate that traffic, so there's no innocent story available for why it fired. That's what makes these alerts high-fidelity: an extremely low false-positive rate, because the alert isn't asking whether something looks bad — it's reporting a fact that is already bad by construction.

An analyst doesn't need to rule out innocent explanations first, the way they would for a firewall or IDS alert. They can treat it as true and move straight to response. The real limitation is worth stating plainly: honeypots only catch attackers who happen to interact with them.

An attacker who never touches the decoy, the share, or the honeytoken walks right past it, undetected. That's real, but it doesn't make deception less valuable — it defines its role. It isn't comprehensive coverage; it supplies a small number of alerts an analyst can trust completely, for exactly the lateral movement other tools often bury in noise.

A SOC triaging ten thousand firewall and IDS alerts a day might see its honeypot fire only twice a month — and every single time, the team investigates immediately, because they already know it's real before checking anything else. Its value was never volume; it was that when it finally speaks, it's always telling the truth. Next up: Chapter 8 begins, designing a segmented network with a DMZ.
